notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Exodus 38 based on the sources I was able to access. I note where I could not find material from certain traditions.

---

## Exodus 38 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### vv. 1–7: The Altar of Burnt Offering

**v. 1:** Bezalel constructed the altar of acacia wood, square (5×5 cubits), 3 cubits high. Ellicott notes this passage corresponds to Exodus 27:1–8 but is somewhat differently worded. The transition is natural from the furniture of the sanctuary to the furniture of the court: first the brazen altar, then the laver.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

Gill simply refers readers to his notes on Exodus 27:1–8, noting the making is ascribed to Bezalel (cf. 2 Chron. 1:5).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

The Pulpit Commentary notes that on completion of the tabernacle, Bezalel and his assistants turned their attention to the court and its furniture, constructing first the altar of burnt offering.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 2:** Horns at each corner, of one piece with the altar, overlaid with bronze. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary both cross-reference Exodus 27:2 and note the horns were integral to the altar structure.

**v. 3:** All utensils (pots, shovels, basins, meat forks, firepans) made of bronze. Ellicott notes "pots" (same word as "pans" in Ex. 27:3) designates the scuttles in which ashes were placed for removal from the sanctuary. The Pulpit Commentary says "pots" is a better translation than "pans" — buckets or scuttles to convey ashes from the altar to the ash-heap (Lev. 1:16).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that in Ex. 27:3 the word "pans" occurs, whereas here it is "pots," which is the more accurate rendering, denoting buckets or scuttles used to carry ashes to the ash-heap.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-38.html

**v. 4:** A grate of bronze mesh was made for the altar under its ledge, halfway up from the bottom. Ellicott notes the order of clauses in vv. 4–5 is changed from the instructions given in Exodus 27, and a distinct statement is made that the rings were "for places for the staves."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**v. 5:** Four bronze rings cast at the four corners of the grate as holders for the poles.

**v. 6:** Poles of acacia wood overlaid with bronze.

**v. 7:** The poles were inserted into the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying. The altar was made hollow with boards.

Grant's Commentary notes: "The copper altar speaks of Christ as the only One whose person is so great that He is able to sustain the responsibility for being the great sacrifice for our sins, for the altar speaks of His person, while every sacrifice was typical of His work of atonement. When first coming into the court, therefore, one would be faced with that which speaks of Christ and Him crucified."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-38.html

David Guzik (Enduring Word) does not add distinct commentary on vv. 1–7 beyond noting they follow the commands of Exodus 27:1–8.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-38/

---

### v. 8: The Bronze Basin

**v. 8:** The bronze basin and its stand were made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.

This verse is the main point of extended commentary across nearly all sources. Several key observations:

**Ellicott:** "Mirrors" (not "lookingglasses") were of burnished metal — bronze plates, round or oval, with a handle, like fire-screens. The women who "assembled" (literally "came by troops") at the Tent of Meeting voluntarily offered their mirrors, which were among their most highly prized possessions. Moses formed their offerings into the most honourable of all the brazen vessels and recorded the fact to the women's credit.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** This fact had not been previously mentioned. Bronze plates admitting a high polish were used by Egyptian women as mirrors from a very early date. The sacrifice of them for a sacred purpose is ascribed to their own self-denying piety rather than to any command by Moses. Women assembled themselves "by troops" at the entrance of the "tent of meeting" set up by Moses (Ex. 33:7). There is no reason to suppose they constituted a regular "order."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**Gill:** Discusses at length the nature of ancient mirrors — not glass but polished metal (brass/bronze). He notes that some interpreters suggested mirrors were affixed around the laver so priests could see their spots when washing, but Gill rejects this because priests washed only hands and feet, not faces. He argues the mirrors were melted down to make the laver. Also notes the women gathered in troops, not necessarily for devotion, but to bring their offerings.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the spiritual application — these women gave up their ability to measure their own physical beauty to make the reservoir for ceremonial washing. "By analogy, it may be said that some are so focused on looking at themselves that they fail to look to Jesus." From a NT perspective, believers experience washing of water by the word (Eph. 5:26), and the word of God is like a mirror (Jas. 1:22–25). Quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "It was highly significant that the brass of these mirrors was employed to construct that laver in which the priests must wash on approaching the altar or entering the Tabernacle. It is in the beauty of holiness men must worship, and by the surrender of everything of the flesh."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-38/

**Precept Austin:** Cross-references Exodus 30:17ff and notes the Hebrew verb translated "served" is rare, used in only one other place of women in sanctuary service (1 Sam. 2:22), and literally means "organized in bands for war" but is used of ordinary Levitical service (Num. 4:23).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-38-commentary

*I was unable to access separate Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, or modern scholarship pages for this verse within the tool limits.*

---

### vv. 9–20: The Courtyard

**v. 9:** The south side — 100 cubits long, curtains of finely spun linen.

**v. 10:** Twenty posts, twenty bronze bases, silver hooks and bands. Pulpit notes "fillets" means "connecting-rods."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 11:** North side identical — 100 cubits, twenty posts, twenty bronze bases, silver hooks and bands.

**v. 12:** West side — 50 cubits, ten posts, ten bases, silver hooks and bands.

**v. 13:** East side — also 50 cubits.

**vv. 14–15:** The entrance curtains on each side were 15 cubits long, with three posts and three bases each.

**v. 16:** All curtains were finely spun linen.

**v. 17:** Bases bronze, hooks and bands silver, plating for tops of posts silver. All posts banded with silver.

Ellicott makes a notable point here: just as in Exodus 36:38 Moses overlaid the capitals of the pillars at the door of the Tabernacle itself with gold, so now he overlaid those at the door of the court with silver — in both cases travelling "beyond the letter of his instructions," probably following his remembrance of the pattern seen on the mount (Ex. 25:9, 40).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

The Pulpit Commentary makes the same observation — this silver overlay was additional to what was recorded in Exodus 27.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 18:** The entrance curtain — embroidered with blue, purple, scarlet yarn and fine linen; 20 cubits long, 5 cubits high. The Pulpit Commentary notes the material was woven of exactly this width.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 19:** Four posts, four bronze bases, with silver hooks, bands, and plating on tops.

**v. 20:** All tent pegs for tabernacle and courtyard were bronze.

---

### vv. 21–31: The Inventory of Materials

**v. 21:** "This is the inventory for the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the Testimony, as recorded at Moses' command by the Levites under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest."

**Gill:** "Sum" refers not to the parts of the tabernacle but to the materials — the gold, silver, and brass — whose weights are given in the following verses. "Tabernacle of testimony" means the tabernacle in which the law, the testimony of the will of God, was put, enclosed in the ark.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**Ellicott:** Translates "sum" as "accounts" or "reckoning." "Tabernacle of testimony" = the dwelling containing God's "testimony" against sin, the Ten Commandments. "For the service of the Levites" means a service they rendered through Ithamar, Aaron's youngest son (Ex. 6:23).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** Notes it is somewhat remarkable that the direction of the Levites was assigned to Ithamar rather than to Nadab or Abihu.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**Precept Austin:** Cites Currid: "For the only time in the book of Exodus, the sanctuary is called the 'tabernacle of testimony.' That is a rare designation in the Old Testament, occurring elsewhere only in Numbers 1:50, 53; 10:11. The term 'testimony' refers to the covenant relationship between God and Israel."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-38-commentary

**v. 22:** Bezalel made everything the LORD commanded Moses.

**Pulpit Commentary:** The direction of the whole work by Bezalel is here asserted more definitely and decidedly than elsewhere.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 23:** Oholiab — an engraver, designer, and embroiderer.

**Ellicott:** "Engraver" is a mistranslation; the Hebrew *khârâsh* means a worker in any material — "artificer." "Cunning workman" literally means "a deviser," especially of textile fabrics. Altogether Oholiab's business was with textile fabrics, not woodwork or metalwork.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Pulpit Commentary** agrees: Oholiab's special gifts were (1) artificer, (2) skilled weaver, (3) embroiderer; his business was with textile fabrics, not wood or metal.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 24:** Gold totaled 29 talents and 730 shekels (sanctuary shekel).

**Ellicott:** Estimates range from £132,000 to £320,000. The amount was remarkable and indicated the liberal spirit of the people. There is "no difficulty" in supposing Israel possessed this gold, since they carried out of Egypt vast amounts of gold and silver ornaments freely given by the Egyptians (Ex. 3:22; 12:35–36).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** Canon Cook estimated £175,075; Thenius about £131,595. Gold was very abundant in Egypt at the period, imported from Ethiopia. If the Israelites numbered two million souls, their gold ornaments would have been worth "very much more than £200,000."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**David Guzik:** Estimates about 2,030 pounds (920 kg) of gold. The present-day value would be part of a total exceeding $13 million. Israel had these resources because they plundered the Egyptians (Ex. 12:36).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-38/

**Gill:** Reckons 29 talents, 730 shekels at £131,595 (Brerewood) or £148,719 (Cumberland). Notes the wealth came from ancestral riches, Egyptian repayment at the Exodus, and spoil from the Red Sea.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**Constable:** Notes slightly over a ton of gold.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-38.html

**v. 25:** Silver from those numbered: 100 talents and 1,775 shekels.

**Pulpit Commentary:** The silver was about four times the weight of the gold but far less valuable — not exceeding £40,000. Gold was more plentiful than silver in early ages in Africa and Asia. This silver was collected by a compulsory tax (the half-shekel census tax of Ex. 30:12–16), whereas the gold was from freewill offerings.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 26:** A beka per person (half a shekel) from 603,550 men aged 20 and older.

**Gill:** Notes the increase of 3,550 men since the Exodus (Ex. 12:37), about six months earlier.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**Ellicott:** "Bekah" means simply "half," restricted in use to the half-shekel. The clause "half a shekel" is probably a later addition to clarify the sense. The census number (603,550) is identical to Numbers 1:46; Ellicott regards both as referring to the same transaction, with the census-taking occupying several months. The Levites were not included.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** The number agrees exactly with Numbers 2:32 (about six months later, excluding 22,000 Levites). Suggests the number may have been "lost in this place, and restored from Numbers 2:32."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/38.htm

**v. 27:** The 100 talents of silver used to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the veil — 100 bases, one talent per base.

**Ellicott:** The sockets of the sanctuary consisted of 40 per side × 2, plus 16 for the west end = 96 total. The sockets of the veil = 4 (supporting the four pillars on which the veil was hung). Total = 100.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Gill:** Each socket cost a talent of silver — according to Dr. Cumberland, about 353 pounds, 11 shillings per socket.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**v. 28:** The remaining 1,775 shekels of silver used for hooks, overlaying tops, and bands for the posts.

**Gill:** Notes the hooks were used for hanging the courtyard curtains. He also records a rabbinic note (Kimchi) that hooks were in the form of the letter *vav* and were used to hang sacrifices for skinning — though Gill notes this refers to second temple practice where hooks were iron, while the tabernacle's were silver.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**v. 29:** Bronze from the wave offering: 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.

**Ellicott:** No great quantity was needed, since bronze was only required for the laver, the altar and its vessels, the sockets of the Tabernacle gate, those of the court, and the pegs.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/38.htm

**Constable:** About two and a half tons of bronze.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-38.html

**Gill:** Notes the bronze may have come from the neighbouring mountains of Arabia where "the metals of brass and iron were first dug."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/38.htm

**vv. 30–31:** Bronze used for bases at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the bronze altar and its grating, all the utensils, bases for the courtyard and its gate, and all tent pegs.

---

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

Within the limited searches I could complete, I found no distinctively Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran, or Anglican commentary on this chapter that differs materially from the traditional readings. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-38.html) was listed but I could not fetch its full content.

The main variation across traditions for this chapter appears in the **spiritual/christological application**, not in doctrinal dispute:

- **Grant's Commentary** (Brethren/Evangelical): Reads the bronze altar as typifying Christ's person, able to "sustain the responsibility for being the great sacrifice for our sins." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-38.html)
- **David Guzik / Enduring Word** (broad Evangelical/Pentecostal): Emphasizes practical application — the mirrors represent self-focus surrendered to God; the exact accounting teaches "thoroughness and accuracy in all things connected with money for religious work." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-38/)

---

**Summary:** Exodus 38 is a largely uncontroversial chapter that narrates the actual construction of the altar, laver, and courtyard, followed by an inventory of metals. Traditional commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik) focus on: (1) the correspondence with the earlier commands in Exodus 27 and 30, (2) the historical details of ancient mirrors in v. 8, (3) the spiritual symbolism of surrendered vanity, and (4) the remarkable wealth and precise accounting of the project. The most discussed verse is v. 8, regarding the women's bronze mirrors used for the laver.
